activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
story:
Hunter stared at the board so hard his eyes ached. Two fractions glared back at him: one quarter plus five twelfths, with a minus sign lurking nearby like a mosquito. He was supposed to figure these out by Friday, and Friday was two days away, which felt like two years.

The real problem was bigger than homework. Ms. Okafor had promised the whole class a pizza party if everyone passed the fractions quiz, and Devin had already announced that if Hunter ruined it for everybody, he would be hiding Hunter's sneakers in the ceiling tiles forever. Hunter had checked the ceiling. Devin could probably reach it.

At lunch, Hunter sat with Priya, who had a pizza slice the size of a door. He had cut his own slice into three skinny pieces because he liked pretending they were three separate snacks. "You wrecked your pizza," Priya said, poking his plate. "Now you have three crumbs."

"No, look." Hunter pushed the three skinny pieces together. They covered exactly the same amount of plate as her one big quarter-sized slice. "Three little pieces, one big piece. Same pizza covered." Priya frowned and dragged her slice over to compare. Same. She cut hers into three too, just to test it, and there they sat, two plates of skinny triangles, identical.

Hunter grabbed a napkin and wrote 1/4. Then, underneath, he drew a pizza cut into twelve slices and shaded three of them. He counted twice, because counting once was for people who had never been burned by a math quiz. "One quarter equals three twelfths," he said slowly, like the words were expensive. "So if the problem has twelfths in it, I can turn my quarter into threths, uh, three twelfths, and then everything matches." Priya said that seemed legitimate to her, since the napkin pizza proved it. Back in class, Hunter raised his hand before the bell even finished ringing. "Can I justify my answer by drawing a pizza on the quiz?" Ms. Okafor said she would accept pizza, but only if the math was right too. On Friday Hunter finished every problem, and when the class average came back high enough for the party, Devin slid the box across the table. "Three slices," he said, cutting a quarter into skinny pieces. "For the genius." Hunter ate them one at a time, like three separate snacks.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
story:
Mason stood at the kitchen counter with seven index cards fanned out like a bad hand of poker. His speech on volcanoes was due Monday, and every time he practiced, he ran out of time before he reached the fifth card.

"You're pacing again," his older sister Priya said from the doorway, gnawing on an apple. She wanted the TV room free by eight for her movie night, and Mason's muttering had been drifting under the door for an hour.

"Seven points. Mr. Okafor said the speech has to be two minutes, and seven points doesn't fit." Mason tapped the cards against the counter. Something was off, but he couldn't see what. He tried grouping them, lining up the two biggest cards on top, making a little hierarchy with the most important fact first. Still too many.

Down the hall, the TV muttered through the wall. Priya had her documentary channel on, and a narrator's voice rolled out: "Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with three Latin words, 'Veni, vidi, vici.'"

Mason walked to the doorway. "Wait, play that back."

Priya paused her apple. "It's a documentary about Rome, not about you."

"Just rewind it."

She sighed, grabbed the remote, and backed it up. Mason listened twice. Caesar had an entire war to talk about, and he'd boiled it down to three short pieces. I came, I saw, I conquered. Three points. Not seven. Not even five. Three, and everyone still remembered them two thousand years later.

He raced back to the counter and tested it, because he didn't fully believe it. He chose his three most influential facts, the ash cloud that blocked the sun, the city buried in a day, the volcano still active today. Then he gave the whole speech to the refrigerator, with a question as his opening hook and his three facts in order. One minute fifty-two seconds. It worked, and for the first time all week it worked on the first try.

He thought about all the afternoons he'd spent cramming in more facts instead of cutting, and he still wasn't sure which approach was really smarter. Priya appeared behind him, keys to the TV room in her hand.

"Done generating noise in my hallway?"

"Done," Mason said, squaring his cards. "I came, I practiced, I conquered."

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
story:
The argument started before the suitcases were even unpacked. "I get the bed by the window," said Hazel's cousin Marcus, planting his backpack on it like a flag. "You always get the window bed," Hazel said. "Last summer, the summer before that, and the summer Grandma made us share the bunk bed and you took the top and drooled on the railing." Their grandfather appeared in the doorway with a rolled-up paper under his arm and a look that meant a story was coming.

"Two brothers fighting over a room," he said. "Reminds me of an empire." He unrolled the paper across the kitchen table and Hazel leaned in. It was a big map, soft at the corners, covered in faded red showing ancient Rome's borders, which stretched so far she had to stand on her toes to see both ends. "The Roman Empire was permanently divided in 395 CE," Grandpa said, tapping the map, "when Emperor Theodosius I died, and his two sons each took one half." He drew his finger down the middle. "East. West." Then he went to check the old wind turbine in the back field, because it rattled when the wind came from the north, and left the map with them.

Hazel traced the border with her finger and thought about it while she chewed her sandwich, letting the whole idea digest: one huge empire, two brothers, one line right down the middle, like tape on a bedroom floor. She grabbed a marker. "Okay," she said to Marcus. "You're the Western half. I'm the Eastern half." He frowned at his half. "Mine's smaller." "That's what you get for drooling on the railing," she said, and drew a squiggle border between the beds.

Later, when the sun went down and the luminous lamp on Grandpa's desk glowed over the paper, Hazel added a tiny drawing in each half: two stick-figure emperors, arms crossed, glaring at each other across the line. When Grandpa came back in with turbine grease on his hands, she slid the map toward him. "Did the brothers glare like this?" she asked. He laughed so hard he had to sit down. "Probably," he said. "Brothers usually do."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
story:
Luke's plan was simple: type a number, see the whole times table spill out in one neat row across the screen. The club demo started in ten minutes, and Mrs. Okoye had promised the best program a bag of Sour Patch Kids.

He drafted his loop fast: ask for a number, then loop from one to ten, printing each answer. "Seven times tables, prepare to be amazed," he whispered, and hit run.

The output climbed down the screen like a staircase. 7, then 14 on the next line, then 21 under that. Ten lines, one number each.

"That's a ladder, not a table," said Priya from the next seat, leaning over. "Rows go sideways."

Luke stared at the code. The loop itself was fine, he was sure of that. So the numbers had to be going onto new lines somewhere he couldn't see, some rule hiding in the print part. He'd made an assumption, he realized, that print just kept going along the same line. Maybe it didn't.

He tested the smallest idea he had: what if print had a way to stay put? He scrolled through his notes and found a line from last week, end=' ' , sitting in an example he'd copied and never used. He slipped it into his print statement and ran it again.

The answers marched across the screen in a single row. 7 14 21 28 35 42 49 56 63 70.

"So print starts a new line every time, unless you put end=' '," Priya read over his shoulder. "Huh. That would have saved me an hour last month."

"You could have told me."

"You called it a ladder with confidence. I assumed you wanted a ladder."

"I'm not that gullible," Luke said, grinning. He added the label, checked the clock, and raised his hand. "Mrs. Okoye, demo's ready."

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
story:
Tristan's mom handed him a crumpled ten-dollar bill right in the middle of the laundromat, between a rattling dryer and a man folding towels. "We need milk," she said. "The corner store. Alone." Tristan's heart did a jump. He had walked there a hundred times, but never by himself, never with his own money to handle.

He raced through the plan in his head while the washers spun in perfect symmetry, two rows of round windows glowing like spaceship portholes. Corner store, milk, change, home. Before he left, he texted his best friend Marcus: "Going to the store SOLO. In charge of money. Wish me luck." Marcus wrote back seconds later: "Don't get robbed by the cashier." Tristan laughed out loud and pushed open the door.

At the store he found the milk, $4.35 on the shelf tag, and marched to the counter. He handed over the ten. The cashier gave him back a five-dollar note, two quarters, a dime, and a nickel. Tristan froze on his way to the door. Was that right? He stood by the gum display and tried something his sister had once shown him: counting up. He started at the price, four thirty-five, then added each coin and note handed back. The nickel made four forty, the dime four fifty, the two quarters five dollars, and the five-dollar note brought it all the way to ten, the amount he had paid. It worked! It matched! He grinned so hard his cheeks hurt.

On the walk home, he decided to modify his route, cutting through the alley to save a whole minute. Then he stopped himself. He was probably a little biased toward shortcuts because they felt adventurous, and his mom had said the main street. He took the main street, milk jug swinging.

He burst back into the laundromat and slapped the receipt on the folding table. "Milk, and I checked the change myself," he announced. "Counting up. Four thirty-five all the way to ten."

His mom raised an eyebrow. "Show me."

"Nickel, dime, two quarters, five," said Tristan, tapping each coin on the table. "Ten dollars, exactly."

"Then you," she said, "are going back for bread tomorrow."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
story:
Michael sat in the reading nook by the window with his notebook, a pencil, and the novel that was due in English class tomorrow. The assignment was one sentence long and somehow harder than a whole worksheet: find the theme of the book and back it up with a quotation from the text. He had an idea about the theme. The main character kept helping people who never thanked him, and still kept doing it, so maybe the book was saying that being kind matters even when nobody notices. The problem was the quotation. He remembered a line from chapter four, something like, "Nobody ever sees what I do for them." He wrote it down, proud of himself, and moved on to the theme paragraph.

Then he stopped. He assumed that quoting from memory would be good enough, but a small wondering crept in: had he really remembered it exactly, or had his brain smoothed it out like a pebble in a creek? He flipped back to chapter four, ran his finger down the page, and found the line. It actually read, "Nobody ever sees half of what I do for them." Two words were wrong, his version and the page's version. He stared at the difference. Half. That word did significant work; it changed the meaning. And a quotation used as evidence had to be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks. He wrote the real line in his notebook, letter for letter, comma by comma, and put quotation marks around it like little fences.

It reminded him of last summer, when he'd tried to bake bread with his grandmother. He'd tossed in flour and water by guesswork because measuring seemed boring, and the loaf had come out flat as a hockey puck. His grandmother hadn't scolded him. She'd just slid the measuring cup across the counter and said, "The recipe doesn't care what you meant." He hadn't understood why that stuck with him until now, sitting here with his pencil hovering over the corrected line.

He looked at his snack plate, where half a peanut butter sandwich sat next to the book. His mother was always saying a sandwich was mostly carbohydrates and he'd need the energy, and right now he did feel like his brain was burning through something. He tested his quotation one more time, reading it against the page word by word. Perfect match. He underlined it twice, wrote the page number beside it, and leaned back into the cushion.

The theme sentence came easily after that, anchored to a line he could point to. He read his paragraph out loud to the empty nook. "The theme is that quiet kindness still counts, because the character says, 'Nobody ever sees half of what I do for them.'" He grinned, closed the notebook, and reached for the other half of the sandwich.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
story:
Maeva sat in the back row of Spanish class with her notebook open and five minutes left before the bell. Friday's quiz would ask everyone to describe their family and pets in full sentences, and Maeva had written one she was not sure about: "Mi hermano está alto." Her brother Thomas really was tall, all elbows and knees, but something about the sentence felt off, the way a shoe feels when it's on the wrong foot.

"You're doing the quiz about pets too, right?" whispered Desmond, who sat beside her. He wanted more than anything to present first on Friday, because his dog Biscuit had learned to roll over and he was hoping the class would beg for a photo. "I already wrote mine. Mi perro es blanco. Five sentences, done."

"That's only one sentence," Maeva said, but she was barely listening. She flipped back through her notes. In September she had written "La profesora está cansada" and gotten it right. In October she had written "Mi madre es maestra" and gotten that right too. Her notebook was turning into a little database of correct sentences, and Maeva began sorting them into two piles in her head, one for es and one for está. Tired went with está. Teacher went with es. White, like Desmond's dog, went with es. She looked for the pattern the way you look for the shape of a constellation: not by staring at one star, but by letting your eyes blur until the lines appear.

Then she saw it, and she grabbed her pen. Everything that lasted, like being tall or being a teacher or being white, used es. Everything that could change by tomorrow, like being tired or being sad or being at school, used está. She crossed out está alto and wrote es alto instead, and she tested the rule against every sentence in her pile. It held. She thought of Thomas, who was impulsive enough to announce that a wrong sentence had called him permanently exhausted, and she laughed out loud before she could stop herself. "Sorry," she whispered to Desmond. "I just realized I almost said my brother is tired forever."

Ms. Rivera looked up from her desk. "Something funny, Maeva?"

"I figured it out," Maeva said, holding up her notebook. "Ser is for lasting traits, estar is for temporary states. That's why my first draft was wrong."

"Good," said Ms. Rivera, checking the clock. "Then you can tell Desmond his dog isn't white every day, either."

Desmond stared at his paper. "Biscuit would never forgive me. Do you have a minute after the bell?"

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
story:
The strawberry box in Grandpa's fridge held four berries, and all of them were pale and enormous, like strawberries that had been taking steroids. Jessica picked one up, sniffed it, and put it back. "Grandpa, why do these cost four dollars in January when the summer ones at the farm stand were two?"

"Because winter strawberries are an insult to the fruit," Grandpa said from his armchair. "They fly them in from somewhere warm, pack them in plastic, and insulate them from any actual flavor." He went back to his crossword.

Jessica had a homework sheet due Monday that demanded an explanation of supply and demand, and she wanted to use strawberries because it was the only example she actually cared about. She spread her paper on the kitchen table and drew two arrows, one going up and one going down, which crossed in the middle like a sword fight. Then she stopped. Somebody must have drawn this crossing-lines thing first, and if a famous person had done it, her teacher would be impressed. She wanted to find out who.

While Grandpa muttered "seven letters, greedy," she went to the bookshelf in the hallway, the one with the books nobody was supposed to touch. One fat old book had a cracked spine the color of an old penny, some kind of copper alloy gone dull. Principles of Economics, it said on the cover. She flipped it open and found the two crossing curves on a page, one slanting down, one slanting up, exactly like her sword fight except neater.

"Grandpa, this book on your shelf. Alfred Marshall, 1890?" She carried it over. "Did you steal this from a museum? Is the author extinct?"

"Economists don't go extinct, they just go out of fashion," Grandpa said, tapping his pen. "That was my university copy. Marshall made those curves famous. Everybody drew them after that."

Now she had her answer, but she still had to prove the strawberry part. She called the farm stand down the road, where a bored teenage voice told her they didn't sell strawberries in winter at all, try again in June. Then she looked up the store flyer for June on Grandpa's ancient computer, which made a noise like a dying lawnmower before it finally loaded. Two dollars a box, June. Four dollars, January. Few strawberries in winter, she wrote, so each one costs more. Lots of them in summer, so the price drops. Then, at the bottom of her sheet, she added one more line: Alfred Marshall put the two crossing curves in his book Principles of Economics in 1890, and made them famous.

She copied his diagram carefully, labeled it S and D, and slid it across the table to Grandpa. He studied it over his glasses, then reached into the fridge, took out one pale winter berry, and set it on her paper next to the curves.

"Four dollars," he said. "Tell your teacher the diagram explains the price, but nothing explains the taste."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
story:
Alexia had practiced her speech eleven times in the bathroom mirror, and every time the mirror looked bored. Today was her first debate tournament, held in the Orange Ridge Middle School library, where posters about democracy hung between shelves and a clock above the door ticked like it was counting down the end of the world. Her topic was whether schools should ban vending machines, and her argument was frugal and airtight: the machines wasted money, they littered the halls, and the school store sold the same snacks anyway. Three points. She had them memorized. What she did not have was a beginning.

The boy who went before her, a tall kid named Deshawn, stood up and said, "Today I will talk about vending machines." Alexia watched the judge's pencil stop moving. She watched the other judge glance at the clock. She watched a girl in the second row pick at her shoelace as if it were the most fascinating object in the library. Deshawn had good points, actually, but by the time he reached them, everyone had drifted off like balloons escaping a birthday party.

Alexia's turn came. "Today I will talk about," she began, and felt the room go gray and floaty, like fog rolling in over the shelves. She stopped. Somewhere in that fog, an idea sparked: the problem wasn't the words after the opening, it was the opening itself. Deshawn had announced his topic instead of grabbing anyone. She took a breath and tried a different door into the room.

"Have you ever found a candy wrapper in your math textbook?" she asked. The shoelace girl looked up. Both judges' pencils hovered. The fog rolled back out through the bookshelves, and the library felt sharp and colorful again, every poster suddenly vivid. She laid out her three points about wasted money, litter, and the school store, and she kept one eye on the judges to monitor whether their pencils were still moving. They were. At the end she said, "So check your textbook, and then check where your money goes."

Afterward, Deshawn found her by the water fountain. "What was that thing you did at the start?" he asked. "My coach calls it a hook," Alexia said. "A question, a surprising fact, or a really short story, and people actually listen." Deshawn wrote something on his notepad, and Alexia leaned over to see what it said. At the top, where his old opening used to be, he had written in careful letters: HOOK FIRST.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
story:
Zoe sat on the hard bench by the teller windows, kicking her sneakers against the tile, while her mother stood in a line that moved like a glacier with lichen on it. Zoe had a math worksheet due tomorrow, and printed at the top was the assignment she'd been dreading: explain supply and demand to the class, using real prices. She had nothing real. She had a pencil and a bank that smelled like paper.

Next to her, her little brother Theo was reading the brochure about certificates of deposit for no reason anyone could determine. "Did you know money can grow?" he said. "It says so right here. It just sits there and grows."

"Nothing just sits there and grows," Zoe said. "Somebody's doing something."

Theo set the brochure down with the air of a man who would not be argued out of a bank document. He could be obstinate about the strangest things. Then he said, "Fine. Then explain why strawberries were four dollars in March and two dollars in June. Nobody did anything. They just got cheap."

Zoe looked at him. "Where? At Renata's stall?"

"At the market. You were there. You ate three samples and bought nothing."

She had been there. In March she'd wanted strawberries so badly she could taste them walking past the stall, and the price had made her buy one sad container and ration it like emergency supplies. In June Renata had practically shoveled them at her, punnets stacked in red towers, two dollars, come on, take two. Zoe had assumed Renata was just being generous, or desperate, or both. But Renata hadn't changed. Something else had.

"The berries," Zoe said slowly, pulling her worksheet onto her knee. "In June they're all ripe outside around here. Renata's got local ones coming in, everyone's got local ones coming in, all at once." She wrote "SUMMER: tons of berries" and drew a wobbly arrow down to "cheap." Then "MARCH: almost none" and an arrow up to "expensive." She tested it against what Theo had seen, like a coin against a counter. Half the price in June. The arrows fit. "It's not that people stopped wanting them," she said. "It's that in March there just aren't that many."

"See, that's doing something," Theo said, waving the brochure. "The strawberries are doing something."

"Berries don't do things. They ripen." Zoe chewed her pencil. Okay, so that was the supply part. The demand part she'd get to later, maybe standing in front of the class, recounting the great strawberry rationing of March and the flood of June, holding up two containers like evidence. Her mother's line finally moved forward one whole person. Zoe flipped the worksheet over and started sketching Renata's stall, the towers of red punnets, and a small stick figure in March, standing alone beside one lonely container, gripping it with both hands.

"Draw me next to her," Theo said. "I'm the one eating the samples."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
story:
The recipe card said twenty minutes at three seventy-five, so Nathan set the little dial on the camper's oven and waited for it to heat. He had already mixed the batter himself, counting the blueberries like treasure, because today was the day he baked muffins from start to finish with no help. His grandpa sat outside in a folding chair, reading, only glancing up when Nathan brought him the egg shells to toss into the fire pit.

The first batch came out black on the bottoms. Nathan scraped them into the trash bag, confused. He had followed every line of the recipe exactly, and the timer had not lied. He mixed a second batch, checked the dial again, and even moved the pan to a higher rack. Those burned too, faster than the first, and the whole camper smelled like scorched blueberries. His eyes stung as he stood at the tiny sink, washing the pan. Grandpa's voice came from the door. "You know, the muffins your uncle made last summer burned in that oven too. And the year before."

Nathan turned that over in his mind. Two different bakers, two different recipes, same burned muffins, same oven. The recipe could not be the problem if it failed the same way for everyone. Maybe the problem was hiding inside the oven itself, where he could not see it. "Grandpa, do you have a thermometer?" he asked. "Not the kind for people. One that could sit inside the oven."

Grandpa dug through a drawer and handed him a round metal oven thermometer with a hook on it. Nathan hung it from the rack, turned the dial to three seventy-five, and waited while the oven hummed and ticked. When he peeked through the glass, the thermometer read four fifty. The dial on the front said three seventy-five, but the actual temperature inside was much hotter. He tested it again at a lower setting and got the same kind of gap. The dial, he realized, did not tell the truth.

So he set the dial lower, watched the thermometer instead, and nudged it until the inside of the oven held close to three seventy-five. The abrupt swings of the dial had fooled him before; the thermometer on the rack did not. He slid in the third batch and set the timer, and this time the kitchen filled with a sweet, toasty smell instead of smoke. When he pulled them out, the muffins were golden, their tops cracked just like the picture on the card. Nathan carried one outside, still warm, and handed it to his grandpa. "Taste it," he said. Grandpa took a big bite, and crumbs fell onto the lichen-covered log beside his chair. "Best one yet," he said, reaching for a second.

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
story:
Addison pressed her back against the cold cinder-block wall of the music room, her folder open to the alto line of "Simple Gifts." Across the room, above the pencil sharpener, someone had taped a leftover science-fair poster with a red warning triangle that read FLAMMABLE, and she stared at it now because staring at anything was easier than singing.

The spring concert was in nine days, and the altos were the problem. When the choir split into two parts, the altos were supposed to hold their lower line against the sopranos' high one, but every time the parts crossed, the whole section wavered like a rope bridge in wind. Addison wanted the moment in the last measure, where the two lines came together on one held note, to sound like a single ribbon of sound. Instead it sounded like two sounds rubbing elbows.

She thought about her grandmother's porch last summer, when two wind chimes hung a few inches apart and never quite agreed. No, that wasn't it. She thought about the tuning fork Mr. Okafor had struck in September, before he'd left on medical leave, and how he'd held it near a piano string. The sound had throbbed, pulsing fast, then slower, then gone smooth. "Listen for the beats," he had told them, and tapped the string's peg a hair sideways. The pulsing had slowed and vanished. She hadn't understood it then. She understood it now, or thought she did, and her heart beat fast enough on its own.

"Alto one and two, just the last note," called Ms. Reyes from the piano. Addison raised her hand. "Can Priya and I try it alone first? Ear to ear, kind of?" Ms. Reyes nodded, curious.

Priya stepped close. They sang the note, and Addison heard it immediately, a wobble in the sound, wob-wob-wob, like a slow heartbeat hiding inside their voices. Somebody was nearly right but not exactly right, and the pulsing was the clue. But which of them? Addison slid her pitch down a sliver. The wobble sped up. She slid back up, past where she'd started, and the pulsing slowed, slowed, then melted away, and the two voices locked into one seamless tone.

"It's gone," Priya whispered, eyes wide. "You fixed it with your ears."

"Both of them," Addison said. "Now the whole section."

They arranged the altos in pairs, ear to ear, and when the choir ran the ending, the last chord bloomed so wide that Ms. Reyes stopped playing entirely, lifted her hands off the keys, and just listened.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
story:
Blake sat on the back steps with his sketchbook, a tennis ball, and a flashlight duct-taped to a lawn chair. Art class had made shading mandatory this quarter, and Mr. Ruiz kept saying Blake's spheres looked like flat pancakes with delusions. Today he intended to fix that.

He propped the flashlight so it hit the ball from the upper left, exactly like the assignment sheet showed. Highlight on the top left, a dark crescent on the right side, and a soft gray blob stretched across the picnic table behind it. He drew it all, then frowned. The shadow side still looked wrong, like a hole in the paper. On a hunch, he made the bottom edge of that dark side almost white, pressing hard with his eraser until it gleamed.

The sphere stopped looking like a sphere. It looked like a ball lit by two flashlights, one from each side. Blake held the drawing next to the real ball and squinted. The real ball's shadow side was not pure black, though. Its bottom edge was faintly lighter, a soft gray, while the middle stayed darkest of all.

"Nadia," he called to his sister, who was pretending to weed but mostly scrolling her phone, "bring me the egg from the fridge. The hard-boiled one."

"You owe me a favor."

"Mandatory favor. Fine."

She brought the egg and lingered, because curiosity is basically a hormone for eleven-year-old siblings. Blake set the egg beside the tennis ball under the same light. Same pattern. story:
Gabrielle stood at the front of the empty classroom holding her note card like it might bite her. Her topic was capybaras, the world's largest rodent, and she had a good opening hook: "Imagine a dog the size of a pig that loves swimming." The problem was that between the hook and the ending, she kept saying one word over and over.

"Um, capybaras can weigh up to a hundred and fifty pounds. Um, they live in South America, um, near rivers." She dropped onto a desk and put her head in her arms. "I sound like a broken robot."

Marcus, who had agreed to be her audience because she'd promised him half her granola bar, held up his phone. "Eleven. That's how many times you said 'um' in two minutes. I counted every single one." He waggled the screen at her. "You want to see the tally? I made little marks. It looks like a fence."

"Delete that fence." She snatched the granola bar out of her backpack, tore off the non-Marcus half, and chewed while she thought. The ums were not random; they showed up in the same places every time, right before each of her three points, like her brain was stalling at the same three stop signs. Maybe the problem wasn't the words coming out of her mouth. Maybe it was the silence she was afraid of. She was stuffing the gaps full of um so nobody would notice she'd paused.

"Okay, new plan," she said. "Count the ums again, but this time I'm going to let the quiet just sit there. If I feel an um coming, I'll shut my mouth instead."

She walked back to the front, planted her feet, and started over. "Imagine a dog the size of a pig that loves swimming." Then she stopped. The room went silent for a second, and it felt enormous, like the whole school could hear her not talking. Her mouth wanted to say um so badly it itched. She kept her lips closed, let the pause do its job, and then delivered her first point clean. Marcus looked up from his phone with his eyebrows raised. She did it again before point two, and again before point three, and somehow the capybara facts landed harder, like each one got a spotlight.

"Two ums," Marcus announced at the end, holding up his phone. "Down from eleven. Also, I actually remembered your whole speech, which never happens." He tapped his tally fence. "The quiet makes you sound like you know what you're doing. Like a confident capybara."

"Those exist?"

"Probably. They're huge. Nobody argues with them."

Gabrielle folded her note card in half and grinned. On speech day, when her name was called, she walked to the front, took one deliberate breath, and said, "Imagine a dog the size of a pig that loves swimming."

Juliette spread the topographic map across the library table, weighting the corners with a dictionary and two atlases. She needed to find the steepest slope of Miller Hill for her geography project, and she only had until the library closed at five. Her friend Dev sat across from her, eating pretzels he was not supposed to have in the building.

The map showed brown squiggly lines all over the hill, like someone had dropped cooked spaghetti on the paper. Juliette counted the lines from the bottom of the hill to the top. "Ten lines," she said. "If each line is fifty feet, that's five hundred feet tall. That's a monster hill." She wrote 500 ft in her notebook and underlined it twice. Dev leaned over, spraying pretzel crumbs. "Miller Hill? My brother sleds there. It takes him ninety seconds to walk up. It is not five hundred feet."

Juliette frowned. Dev's brother was annoying but not a liar. She traced the lines with her finger, thinking that the lines on the west side of the hill bunched together like a squeezed accordion, while the east side spread out in lazy loops. She had read somewhere that the steepest part was wherever the lines crowded closest together. She tapped the western slope. "The lines cooperate here," she said, pointing at how they stacked neatly side by side. "That's the steep side." Dev snorted. "Lines don't cooperate. Lines just lie there." "They cooperate with each other. Look, they're all pressed together."

But the five hundred feet still bothered her. She turned the map over, checked the corners, and finally found the legend, a small box of tiny print she had walked past twice. There it was: "Contour interval 40 feet." The contour interval is the difference in height between one contour line and the next, and it is printed right there in the legend. She had guessed fifty. She was wrong. "Forty feet," she said. "Ten lines means four hundred feet. I would have gotten it wrong." She crossed out her number, and Dev did a vigorous fist pump, as if he had personally won an argument, even though he had contributed nothing but crumbs.

Then came the twist. Under the legend, in even smaller print, was a note that the map had been redrawn in 1998, after the quarry on the north face had cut the hill down. The old map in the atlas beside her showed eleven lines, not ten. "The hill shrank," Juliette said. "The map is newer than the atlas. So it's four hundred now, not four hundred forty." Dev looked at the pretzel in his hand, then at the map, then at the clock. "Can I see the legend? I want to check whether there's a tariff on overdue atlases too."

Arianna's father had said she could join the lake swim at Maya's birthday party on Saturday, but only if she could make it across the backyard pool, twenty-five metres, front crawl with side breathing. Tonight was her last practice, and the pool floats and the ladder were still piled at the deep end where they could obstruct her path. Her cousin Theo agreed to stand at the corner with a stopwatch and a whistle.

Her first try failed at the halfway rope. Every time she needed air, she lifted her face forward out of the water, and by the time she reached the rope her legs felt heavy and slow, dragging low behind her. Theo blew the whistle. "Twenty-two seconds to the rope, then you stopped," he called. "You're kicking aggressive enough to power a boat. Something else is wrong." Arianna floated on her back, thinking. She couldn't see herself swim. Whatever was slowing her down was happening under the surface, hidden from both of them.

She tried a test. She pushed off easy and swam ten strokes without breathing at all, face straight down. Her legs rode high. Then she lifted her head forward for one breath, and she felt it at once: her hips dropped, her legs sank, and her whole body seemed to plow instead of glide. "It's the looking up," she gasped at the wall. "When I lift my head forward to breathe, my hips and legs sink and everything drags. If I turn my head to the side instead, my body stays flat." She tugged her goggles tighter over the soft cartilage of her nose and set her feet against the wall.

Theo raised the whistle. "One shot. Party's Saturday."

She pushed off, arms turning, and when she needed air she rolled her head sideways, one ear in the water, and found the gap. Flat and fast, she passed the rope, passed the ladder, and slapped the far wall.

Theo leaned over the edge, grinning. "Twenty-five metres. Forty-one seconds."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
story:
Elena slid into the last row of folding chairs at the town hall, balancing her skateboard against her knee. She had come with one question, and she had written it on an index card so she wouldn't lose her nerve.

The meeting opened with pothole reports, then a long argument about a fence on Maple Street. Elena waited. When the chairperson called for public questions, she stood up.

"Senator Doyle," she began, then stopped, because the man at the front table wasn't a senator at all. He was Mr. Okafor, who ran the hardware store and sat on the town council.

"Just councillor is fine," he said, and a few people laughed kindly.

Elena tried again. "The park by my community centre has signs that say no skateboarding. I checked, and the park right outside Riverton, five minutes past the town line, has a skate bowl. Same kind of park. So why is it legal there and not here?"

"Because our no-skateboarding rule is a bylaw," Councillor Okafor said. "A bylaw is a rule made by a local government, like our town council, and it applies only within this municipality."

Elena sat down and turned the words over. Only within the municipality. The rule wasn't a national law that everyone had to follow; it was something this town had decided, which meant this town could decide something different. Her inference was simple: if people made the rule, people could change it. But she wanted to test it before she trusted it.

She raised her hand again. "If I wanted the bylaw changed, what would I actually do? Like, what are the steps?"

"You'd submit a petition," the councillor said. "Signatures from residents, a written request, delivered to the clerk's office. Then it gets on a council agenda, and you'd speak for three minutes at a meeting like this one."

"How many signatures?"

"Twenty-five is the minimum."

After the meeting, Elena found Councillor Okafor by the coffee urn. She asked whether petitions from kids counted, and he said signatures counted if the signer was a resident, whatever their age. Then he added something she hadn't expected.

"You know who originally asked for that ban?" he said. "A petition. Eleven years ago. Skateboards on the paths, seniors complaining about near misses. It wasn't arbitrary."

Elena stood there holding her index card. The rule she wanted gone had been created by the exact tool she was about to use. She had assumed someone in charge had just decided, top down, and that was wrong.

She spent the next two weeks at the community centre with a clipboard. Some adults refused to sign, saying the boarders were a nuisance, which was subjective, since other adults signed while calling the same riders harmless. Twenty-two signatures in, she stalled for three days. She persisted anyway, coming back after school, until a woman who'd refused twice looked at the list, sighed, and wrote her name.

On the agenda for the next meeting, item six: petition 2024-31, skateboard access, Rotary Park. Elena sat in the front row this time, index card face down on her lap.

story:
Samuel stood at the kitchen counter with three crumpled bills and a note from his mom. "Two liters of milk," it said, "and don't lose the change." She was supervising from the doorway in her bathrobe, pretending to wash a mug that was already clean.

"Can I actually go alone this time?" he asked.

"You're twelve," she said. "The store is at the corner. Yes."

The walk took four minutes. Samuel counted them, because counting made the street feel smaller. At Delgado's Market the milk cooler hummed, and a hand-lettered sign read MILK 2.65. He carried two liters to the register, where a teenager with a name tag that said DEREK slid them into a bag.

"That'll be two sixty-five," Derek said, holding out his palm.

Samuel gave him the five-dollar bill from the note. Derek punched at the register, frowned at it, and handed back two coins and a one-dollar bill.

Outside, on the curb, Samuel counted. One dollar, one quarter, one dime. One dollar thirty-five. He sat very still, because something didn't fit, and he could see the whole thing in his head like a math problem written on air. Milk was two sixty-five. He had paid five. Five dollars take away two sixty-five... he borrowed a ten from the five's place, made it fourteen, and it came out two dollars and thirty-five cents. Two thirty-five, whatever the money was made of, quarters or dollars or coins from a board game. Derek had given him a dollar short.

Back inside, Samuel set the bag on the counter. "I think the change is wrong," he said. "Milk is two sixty-five, I paid five, so it should be two thirty-five."

Derek squinted at his register. "It says one thirty-five."

"Maybe the machine made a mistake," Samuel said. "Like a diagnosis. Even computers get sick."

Derek laughed, then counted it out by hand, coin by coin, and his eyebrows went up. "Huh. You're right." He dug another dollar from the drawer and slapped it into Samuel's palm. "You should come back every Saturday. You're kind of influential around here now."

Samuel walked home holding the bag against his chest, and at the kitchen door he laid out the coins in a neat line on the counter, two thirty-five exactly, like evidence.

His mom looked at the row of coins, then at him. "Well?" she said.

"Next week," said Samuel, "I'm buying the bread too."

Priya stood up. "That's it. That's the thing underneath the words. Ms. Alvarez calls it subtext."

"Subtext," Grace repeated, tasting it. She flipped to a clean page and wrote it at the top, then wrote pause, hands, crack beside her lines.

She ran it once more, slower still, and this time she heard someone in the dark rows sniffle.

"Priya?"

"I'm fine," came the wobbly answer. "Really."

story:
Hudson had exactly forty minutes before his dad picked him up, and one worksheet that said, in cheerful teacher handwriting, "Explain the pyramids AND the Nile. In your own words." He stood in front of a model of Giza, all sand and tiny stone triangles, and felt his brain begin to decompose on the spot.

"The gift shop closes at four," said his sister, Priya, who had her own agenda and had stated it eleven times since the parking lot.

"Two minutes." Hudson circled the model. The pyramids sat on the west side of the Nile, and the little farms sat right on the river's edge, green strips squeezed against blue. That was the pattern. The fields needed to be near the water because the water was everything, and the tombs rose on the far bank like they'd been parked there on purpose. Floods, he guessed, were a signal, the calendar the whole country ran on. When the river rose and then dropped, it left wet soil, and the farmers planted in that. But the river dropped a lot. How did a field get water when it sat higher than the water did?

The next room answered him, though not in words. A tall pole was pivoted on a wooden frame, with a rope and bucket hanging from one end and a blob of clay on the other. A plastic tub of water sat below it, a raised sandbox above. A sign gave one line: Try it. A docent leaned against the wall looking impartial, as if this were not the most interesting object in the building.

Hudson pulled the rope down. The bucket dipped into the tub. When he let go, the clay end dropped and the whole thing swung up, and the bucket of water rose without him doing anything. He swung it over the sandbox and tipped it into the sand, which darkened in a spreading circle.

"It's called a shaduf," the docent said. "The weight does the lifting."

Priya appeared beside him, gift shop apparently forgotten. "Let me do one." She pulled the rope, hauled up a bucket, and dumped it on Hudson's shoe.

"That was the field," Hudson said, wringing out his sock. "Very fertile."

Benjamin stood in the middle of the empty school auditorium with a photocopy shaking in his hand. Monday was the audition for the spring showcase, and he wanted the drama club solo slot more than he wanted recess, maybe more than he wanted pizza Friday. The problem was his speech. "To be, or not to be," he recited for the tenth time, then stopped. It sounded flat, like he was reading a cereal box. His friend Priya sat in the third row, chewing her pencil.

"You're rushing it," she said. "Try stopping after the comma. Like the thought is too heavy to carry."

He tried again. "To be... or not to be." The pause made the words feel like they were falling into a hole. He grinned. It was working! But then Priya asked which play it came from, and he froze. He knew it was Shakespeare, and he knew the character was Hamlet, but when she asked where it sat in the play, he had to admit he didn't know.

"That's the negotiation," Priya said, tapping her pencil on the armrest. "Ms. Ruiz asked me yesterday. If you can't say where it comes from, she'll think you just picked something famous without doing the work."

Benjamin raced to the library before it closed and pulled the fat Hamlet book off the shelf. He flipped pages, hunting. There it was, and the scene heading told him everything: the speech sat in Act 3, Scene 1. He had assumed it came near the beginning because it was so famous, and he was wrong. Famous things didn't have to come first, he realized; they just had to be good.

Monday came fast. When Ms. Ruiz asked him where his speech belonged, Benjamin stood tall, no longer wanting to hide behind the copy in his hand.

"It's a soliloquy," he said, "from Act 3, Scene 1 of Hamlet." Then he lifted his hand slowly, the way he had practiced, letting the silence do half the talking. "To be... or not to be."

Emile stood barefoot on the lanai of his Auntie Leilani's house, arms heavy, feet tangled. In three weeks he was supposed to dance at the community festival, and so far he could not get through a single verse without stopping.

At home he had practiced by humming the melody the way he practiced songs for choir, finding the tune in his head and letting it carry him. His cousin Nalu sat on the steps watching, shaking her head. "That's why you keep losing your place," she said. "You're not dancing to a song. This is hula kahiko. It goes with chanting and a gourd drum, not a sung melody."

Emile frowned. Last summer flashed back to him: Auntie pounding a rhythm on a hollowed gourd while the older kids danced, their movements sharp and grounded, and no music at all, just voices rising and falling in a chant. He had thought then that they were dancing without music. Now he understood the chant was the music, and his humming was a different song entirely.

So he tested it. Instead of humming, he chanted the words out loud, quietly, and let Auntie's drum, the deep boop and slap of the gourd against the mat, be his only clock. When his knees kept sinking low on the wrong beat, he guessed the problem: he was counting in his head instead of listening. He stopped counting. He followed the drum alone, letting the chant's words tell his hands where to go. The movements that symbolize wind and rain began to feel like wind and rain, not like a list of positions.

"Better," Nalu called out. "Your timing is consistent now. You're with the drum."

Auntie brought out a folded mat for the cold evening, wrapping one edge around Emile's shoulders like insulation against the trade wind, and he laughed and shook it off, because he was warm from working.

He started the verse again, feet striking the boards in time, and this time when the drum paused for a breath, he paused too, arms still, waiting for the chant to rise.

"One more time," said Auntie, lifting the gourd.

Emmett stood in Grandma's kitchen holding a spoon like a microphone, and for the fourth time he forgot his own second sentence.

"Grandma, can I practise on you again?"

She set down her crossword. "Again and again until it's boring. That's how your grandpa learned his wedding speech, and he only forgot the ring, not the words."

The problem was real. Tomorrow night Emmett had five minutes at the township council meeting to argue against the new bylaw that would tear out the community garden behind the recreation centre, where he had grown the lush rows of beans and zucchini that had won him a ribbon at the fall fair. The bylaw said the land would become extra parking. Emmett had learned, from a page on the township website he'd found while sulking about it, that residents could ask to speak briefly at a council or committee meeting. It was called appearing as a delegation. He'd filled out a form, emailed it in, and gotten a reply giving him a spot. Five minutes, no more.

"You're pacing," Grandma said. "Why don't you stand still and imagine the councillors are bean plants? You've talked to bean plants all summer."

"I have never talked to bean plants."

"You narrated to them. I heard you. You said, and I quote, grow, you stubborn little polymer sacks of water."

Emmett laughed so hard he lost his place on the notecards again. "Cells aren't polymer sacks. Well, the cell walls sort of are, actually. Cellulose is a polymer." He frowned at the cards. "That's not the point. The point is I keep trying to memorize every word, and then one word falls out and the whole speech collapses like wet cardboard."

He thought about the fair, back in September, when the judge had asked him a question he hadn't prepared for. What had he done? He hadn't recited anything. He'd just answered, plainly, about how he'd composted and watered. It had worked because he was talking about something he actually knew.

"Grandma, what if I don't memorize it? What if I just know three things I want to say, in order, and say them like I'm answering the bean question?"

"Then say them to me right now, and I'll be a grumpy councillor who wants more parking."

Emmett put the notecards face down on the counter. "Councillors, seventy families grew food in that garden this year. Parking is something we can generate anywhere, but that soil took us eight years to build. Tomorrow I'm appearing as a delegation, so you have to hear me out, and here is why you should keep the garden."

He went through it twice more, no cards, once while Grandma heckled him about parking. When he finished, she stood up and applauded with her oven mitts.

"I have my own request, by the way," she said. "While you're at that meeting, ask them to fix the streetlight at my corner. I've written three letters. Maybe a delegation gets somewhere."

"Deal," Emmett said, and picked the spoon back up.

The petition lay flat on the counter at city hall, all four pages of it, held down by Jaxson's elbow so the fan by the clerk's window wouldn't flip it over. Behind him, Mira and Devon shifted from foot to foot in their school backpacks. They had collected one hundred and six signatures in eleven days, standing outside the library and the corner store with clipboards, asking people to sign so the city would put a crosswalk on Hartley Road where the middle school kids jaywalked every afternoon because the nearest crossing was three long blocks away.

"I can't take that here," the clerk said, tapping her pen toward a doorway marked Council Services. "Third floor. Ask for the clerk of council." Jaxson picked up the pages. The top sheet had gone slightly translucent from the drizzle that morning, and you could see the signature on the reverse side showing through, backward, like a ghost of itself.

On the third floor, the clerk of council read the pages slowly, and Jaxson's stomach knotted, because he had written the request himself and he was suddenly sure he'd done it wrong. "You've got signatures," the woman said, "but you haven't said what you want them to do. A petition is a written request, signed by many people, asking a government body to take a specific action. Yours says the road is dangerous. That's a complaint, not a request."

Devon made a small noise, and Jaxson felt heat crawl up his neck, the embarrassment of having walked a hundred and six people into a dead end. But then he thought about it the way he thought about math problems, backward from the answer. They had the signatures. Those were still good. Kate stood at the soup vendor's table at the Saturday farmers' market, holding a wooden spoon like it might bite her. "Sort of," Kate said. "Look at that," Mrs. Okafor said. "No lumps at all."

Kate stared at the pot. "So the darker I cook it, the less it thickens. The browning must break down the flour's starch." She said it slowly, testing the idea against Tuesday's cheese water, and it fit.

story:
Luca knelt at the edge of the inflatable pool his dad had set up on the lawn, holding a garden hose he'd stretched along the grass. Twenty-five metres. That was the distance, and next Saturday was the club's test to move up from the beginners group. The pool wasn't even three metres long, so swimming it here was impossible. He would have to figure out the hard part, the side breathing, some other way.

The hard part was this: every time he turned his head to breathe, he swallowed water instead of air. He had a theory about why. Maybe the problem wasn't the turning. Maybe his arm was splashing water right where his mouth went, so the water was already there before he turned. He couldn't see it himself, but his little sister Priya was watching the Olympics on the tablet on the porch, and she could watch him.

"Why does everyone in that race do the same stroke?" Luca asked, nodding at the screen. "It says freestyle. I thought that meant you could pick any one."

"You can pick any one," Priya said. "Almost all swimmers choose front crawl because it's the fastest of the competitive strokes."

Luca stared at the swimmers churning down the lanes, all of them rolling their heads sideways like gears in a machine. Then he looked at the pool. "Priya, come here. Watch my right arm when I breathe. Tell me if it splashes."

He lay flat in the shallow water and mimicked the stroke in slow motion, pulling his arm, turning his head. Priya leaned close, frowning like a scientist. "It's not the arm," she said. "You're lifting your head up first, then sideways. Your face is going forward and up at the same time. That's why you get water."

Lifting then turning, instead of just turning along the water like the Olympic swimmers did. That was a pattern he could test. He tried again, keeping one cheek pressed to the surface like a pillow, one goggle in the water and one out. Air came in. Real air, no coughing. "It worked," he said, spitting a little grass out of his mouth anyway.

Afterward he sat dripping on the step and helped Priya retrieve the tablet charger from under the couch cushion on the porch, since she'd promised to time him in exchange. "When I pass the test," Luca said, "I'll be in the older group. Real laps, real races."

"Will you do freestyle like everybody else?"

Luca thought about it. He had always imagined doing something different, a fancy stroke nobody expected. "I changed my mind," he said. "If almost everyone picks front crawl because it's fastest, then that's the credible choice, isn't it? You'd have to have a really good reason not to."

"You could have a good reason," Priya said. "You could want to lose slowly in style."

Luca laughed so hard he fell backward into the pool, and came up doing three strokes, breathing sideways, all the way to the far wall.

story:
Tyler had forty minutes before his grandmother arrived to drive the volcano to the science fair, and the volcano had fizzed exactly once all afternoon. He stood at the kitchen counter between a box of baking soda and a bottle of vinegar, glaring at both of them like they owed him money.

His little sister Nadia sat on the counter, allegedly helping. "Do it again," she said.

"I can't just do it again. The fair starts at seven." Tyler peered into the bottle. The baking soda had slid down in a wet lump, and the bubbles had vanished like they were never there. He thought about the iron gate behind the garage, the one he'd photographed in September for his poster. In September it had been gray. By December the bottom rungs were orange and flaky, and no amount of scrubbing had turned the orange back to gray. That was the whole reason he'd picked this project: some things you could undo, like melting butter and pouring it back into a dish to harden, and some things you couldn't. He'd tested the butter on Tuesday and his mother had tested his patience on Wednesday when she found the dish.

"The bubbles," Nadia said, pointing at the dead bottle. "Where'd they go?"

"Out. Bubbles go out."

"Where'd they come from?"

Tyler opened his mouth to say something and found nothing in there. He'd watched the fizz rise a hundred times in videos, and he'd never once asked himself where it began. The poster on the table had a section he'd labeled with duct tape: WHAT PROVES A CHANGE IS REAL. Under it he'd glued the gate photo and a drawing of butter. Nothing about bubbles. Nothing about the one thing his volcano actually did.

He grabbed the tape and peeled the section off, then wrote a new heading: SIGNS OF A CHEMICAL CHANGE. He set out two cups. In the first he put a spoon of butter and softened it in his hands, because he still needed the melt comparison, and the oven took too long. In the second he dropped a pinch of baking soda and drizzled vinegar over it. Fizz. He drizzled more. Fizz, fizz, a robust column of it, better than the volcano had ever managed.

"There," Nadia said. "Do the bubbles mean it's working?"

"They mean the stuff turned into new stuff." He held the cup out to her so she could see the bubbles climbing the sides. "Gas bubbles when two things mix, like baking soda meets vinegar, are a sign a chemical change happened. That's what the fizz is. It's my proof."

"That's it? That's the whole proof?"

"That's the whole proof, and it's better than my butter."

The clock said 6:22. He funneled fresh baking soda into the cone, positioned the vinegar, and carried the poster flat like a pizza. At the door he stopped, went back, and dropped a carrot into his backpack, because the class rodent, Biscuit, was riding along, and Biscuit did not care about chemical changes, only about dinner.

"Start the car, Grandma," he called. "I'm bringing the volcano, the butter, and a rodent."

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
story:
Raphael stood on Mr. Lin's porch with a crumpled note in his pocket and a bag of dumplings in his hand. His friend Dara had gone inside already, and now Mrs. Lin was talking to him in quick Mandarin that flew past like sparrows. He caught nothing. Last summer he had nodded along at his grandfather's market walks, pretending to understand, and the memory of that humiliation still made his ears hot. This time he wanted real words.

"Zǒu ba," Dara called, waving him toward the door. "That means let's go."

They walked to the market behind Mrs. Lin, who carried an empty basket on her arm. When they reached the corner, she stopped and asked Raphael a question with a rising twist at the end. He heard two words he almost knew, but the market had two doors, one to the left and one to the right, and he had no idea which one she meant. Dara looked at him, waiting.

Raphael thought back to those walks with his grandfather. There had been a game of it, once: the old man pointing left and saying "zuǒ," pointing right and saying "yòu." The words had not sounded the same at all, and Raphael had always assumed that was just his bad ear. But now, listening to Mrs. Lin repeat the question, he noticed something. One word dipped down like a slide, and the other rose and circled. Maybe each direction had its own sound, its own tune, and the tune was part of the word itself. That was a pattern he could test.

He pointed at the left door and said, carefully, the dipping one: "Zuǒ?"

Mrs. Lin's whole face opened. "Duì! Zuǒ means left," she said, and she pointed with him, then swung her finger the other way. "Yòu means right." She said it again, slower, and Raphael heard the rise and circle of the second word clearly now, as if the sound itself were pointing.

They went in the left door. The market smelled like ginger and dried mushrooms, and Mrs. Lin filled her basket with bean sprouts that rattled like rain. Raphael tried his two words at the tea stall, pointing at jars: zuǒ, yòu. The stall keeper laughed and slid him a cup of something sweet. He had spent a whole summer nodding and understanding nothing, and he wondered, holding the warm cup, whether that had been his fault or just a choice he could make differently now. He could not decide, and it did not seem to matter as much as it once had.

On the walk home, Dara tested him at every turn. "Which way?"

"Zuǒ," Raphael said, and turned left, and behind them Mrs. Lin called out, "Yòu! Your house is on the right," so he laughed and turned the other way.

Gavin's stomach growled so loudly that his cousin Dana snickered across the table. Shabbat had started at sundown the night before, and this was his first time trying to keep the whole day of rest, no snacks between meals, no video games, no rushing around. He had devised a plan at breakfast: whenever he wanted his tablet, he would find one person at Aunt Miriam's house and ask them a question instead. It had worked six times so far. The seventh time, he asked his grandfather why the day of rest ended with a whole ceremony instead of just, well, ending.

"You'll see," Grandpa said, which was the most annoying answer in the world.

Ruthie held out both hands. Her chin was up, but Gavin could see her fingers trembling as the flame caught and light jumped against the cabinets. They passed around a little silver box of fragrant spices, and Gavin breathed in cloves and something sharp and sweet. The smell was supposed to carry you through the week, Dana whispered, like saving up the rest day in your nose.

Gavin thought about his empty morning, the hungry hours, the six questions. It had felt like nothing was happening. But something had been happening the whole time, the way the braided candle had one flame made of several wicks, and you couldn't see where one part ended unless you looked hard.

Ruthie dipped the candle into the wine and the flames hissed out.

"I did it," she said. "Next year, can I hold the cup too?"

Max had signed up for art elective the moment the signup sheet went up, because today was the day they got to draw with real charcoal, and he'd been talking about it since breakfast. "Everyone gets a Styrofoam ball and a lamp," Dana announced, plunking a box of balls on the table. "Today we're drawing spheres, and the goal is to make them look solid. Not like flat circles. Like balls sitting on the table."

Max grabbed his ball and set it on the picnic table while Dana positioned the lamp at the side. The light hit the ball on the upper left, leaving a bright spot there and a darker curve opposite. He squinted at it, then at his page, and started drawing. Circle first. Then he shaded the right side darker, kept the upper left light, and smudged everything with his thumb until it looked smooth.

"What do you think?" he asked his friend Theo, who was sitting across from him drawing his own ball.

Theo leaned over. "It's good, but something's weird. Yours looks like it's floating. Like a planet."

Max held his drawing up next to the real ball. Theo was right. His ball looked round, sure, but it hung above the table instead of resting on it. He hadn't even drawn a shadow yet. He sketched a gray oval spreading out from the base and filled it in lightly.

"Still floating," Theo said.

Max frowned at the real ball again. The lamp came from the side, so the shadow stretched away from it, but it wasn't all the same gray. He crouched down until his eyes were level with the tabletop. Right where the ball curved down and met the wood, the shadow went nearly black. He looked at his own drawing. He had made his shadow oval one even, symmetrical gray, like a sticker.

He pressed his charcoal hard onto the page right at the point where his drawn ball touched the drawn table, then dragged it just a tiny bit sideways, fading quickly. He lifted the paper.

"Whoa," Theo said. "It's sitting. It's actually sitting on the table."

Max laughed out loud. "The darkest part is right where it touches! Almost no light gets into that little gap!" He shaded his floating-looking first attempt the same way, dark at the contact point, and watched that one sit down too.

At the end of the session, Max petitioned Dana to let the class hang their spheres on the craft cabin wall, and she said yes before he even finished asking. He pinned his drawing up, stepped back, and grinned at the ball that finally, definitely, was not going anywhere.

Autumn had read The War That Saved My Life twice, and she was sure the theme was about courage, but Mr. Delgado had written one word on her last English essay: evidence? So tonight at book club, in the corner of the library with the squishy blue chairs that smelled faintly of orange cleaner, she was going to find a quotation that proved it.

She flipped through her paperback, past the dog-eared pages, until she found the passage she loved, the one where Ada finally rides Bones across the field even though her conscience tells her she'll be in trouble if her mother finds out. It was beautiful. It was also, she realized as she copied it into her notebook, extremely long. She counted the lines. Nine. Far more than four.

"What are you frowning at?" asked Priya, leaning over with a granola bar in one hand. "Did the book kill somebody again?"

"Worse. MLA," Autumn said, and Priya snorted so hard a crumb landed on the chapter list. Last month Autumn had assumed she could just stuff any quotation inside a sentence with quotation marks around it, like a marshmallow in a s'more. Mr. Delgado had circled her giant quotation and written see me, which was scarier than any villain in the novel.

So she tested it. She wrote her two favorite lines inside her paragraph with quotation marks and it looked fine. Then she wrote out the full nine-line passage the same way, and it was a disaster, a wall of quotation marks that swallowed her whole sentence like a python swallowing a beach ball.

Priya grabbed the MLA handbook from the shelf behind them and thumbed through it, chewing. "Here. In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks."

"No quotation marks at all?"

"Not one."

Autumn tried it. She moved the whole passage onto its own lines, indented half an inch from the margin, and took off the quotation marks. Suddenly her paragraph could breathe, and the passage just sat there, eloquent and sure of itself, backing up her theme like a friend standing behind her.

When it was her turn to share, Autumn read her theme, then the blocked passage, then said, "Courage isn't the absence of fear. It's acting anyway."

Mr. Delgado, stacking chairs nearby, looked over. "Evidence?" he asked.

Autumn held up her notebook and tapped the indented block. "Right there."

Florence sat in the plastic chair at Wanderlust Travel while her mother compared packages at the front desk. Behind the agent's computer hung a huge world map with faint lines drawn across it, and along the top and sides ran numbers: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180. A small monitor on the counter listed flights, and next to each city was a pair of numbers. Lagos: 6, 3. Kathmandu: 27, 85. Honolulu: 21, 157.

Her grandmother lived in Kathmandu, and Florence wanted to find it on the map before Mom finished paying. She picked up the ruler from the agent's desk drawer, held it against the map, and tried to calibrate it against the numbers along the top, matching one ruler mark to every ten degrees. But which number was which? The screen gave her 27 and 85 with no labels at all.

She traced the horizontal lines first. They were numbered from 0 at the equator up toward the poles, and Lagos sat at 6, near the fat middle of Africa. So the first number on the screen matched those. That left 85 for the lines that ran up and down. She counted them out from the line marked 0, which the map labeled the prime meridian, and they climbed to 90, then 150, then 180, and on the other side of the map they climbed again from 0 to 180 the other way.

"So that's longitude," she said, mostly to herself.

The agent looked over. "That's what it's called," she said, and went back to the paperwork.

Florence followed the up-and-down line numbered 85 east of the zero line, then the horizontal line numbered 27, and where they crossed she found Kathmandu, a dot inside Nepal. She put her fingertip on it just as her mother turned around.

"We leave in March," Mom said. "Three weeks."

"Good," Florence said. "I already know right where she is."

The store was four blocks away. Everly counted the crosswalks, waited for the walk signal at each one, and felt the five dollars crinkle in her pocket like a small transmitted message from her mother. On the shelf, the milk was marked $3.99. She did the math twice on her finger on the way to the register: five dollars minus $3.99 left one dollar and one cent. The cashier, a woman with a name tag that said Rosa, rang it up, and the screen showed $4.31.

"Wait," Everly said. "The shelf says $3.99." Her cheeks went hot. She had counted, she had checked, and she was thirty-two cents short of what she'd expected, even though she still had enough. Rosa pointed at the receipt line that said TAX. Then a man behind Everly, holding bread, leaned in with a gentle smile. "Happened to me for years," he said. "I moved here from England. In the UK and EU, the price on the shelf already includes VAT, so what you see is what you pay. Here in the US and Canada, shelf prices leave out sales tax, and they add it at the till."

Everly stared at the numbers. So that was the rule: the shelf price was only part of the truth, and the till finished the sentence. She tested it in her head with the candy bar by the register, marked $1.00. If the same rate applied, it would cost $1.08 at the register, not a dollar even. She had a dollar in quarters in her other pocket, and she slid them across the counter. The screen read $1.08. "I'm eight cents short," Everly said. Rosa popped the candy into the bag anyway. "For walking here all by yourself," she said.

Everly carried the milk home past the crosswalks, the receipt folded in her fist so she could study the little TAX line again. At the driving school, her mother was standing beside a student car, waving. Everly held up the receipt like a trophy. "Shelf prices lie," she announced, "except in England."

story:
William's cousin Kayla had a credit card balance of two hundred dollars, and she had stopped using the card entirely, but somehow the balance kept growing every month. "It's like the debt is alive," she told him at lunch, slamming her locker in the hallway outside the cafeteria. William couldn't stop thinking about it through math class. Something invisible was feeding it.

That afternoon, Mr. Ruiz assigned a project: compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first. William chose the skateboard he wanted, one hundred eighty dollars, as his example. He spread his notes across the library table and drew two columns. If he saved twenty dollars a month from mowing lawns, he'd have the board in nine months, and it would cost exactly one hundred eighty dollars. If he borrowed the money on a card instead, he'd pay interest every month he didn't clear the balance. He copied the numbers down, month by month, his pencil slowing.

Then he saw it, and his stomach dropped. The first month's interest got added to what he owed. The second month, interest was charged on that bigger number, which meant interest was being charged on interest. Each row of his table grew by more than the row before it. The debt wasn't just growing, it was accelerating, like a seed that had germinated in the dark and was now pushing up faster every day. He tested it twice, redrawing the table on a fresh sheet because he was sure he'd fractured one of his own calculations somewhere. Both tables came out the same. The numbers didn't lie.

He found Kayla by the buses after school. "The interest they add becomes part of what you owe," he said. "Then the next month's interest is charged on that interest too. That's why your balance climbs even though you never use the card." Kayla stared at him, then at her phone, where her statement confirmed every step.

"So it's not extravagant spending anymore," she said quietly. "It's the debt feeding itself."

William folded his tables and put them in his backpack. "Save first," he said, and started walking home to plan his lawn schedule.
